detail.title: How AI Anchor Characteristics Influence Purchase Intention: A Moderated Mediation Model Based on SOR Theory
detail.abstract: ​ To investigate how and under what conditions AI-powered virtual anchors influence consumers’ purchase intention,Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework, this study builds a moderated mediation paradigm.Virtual anchor characteristics—professionalism, interactivity, and attractiveness—are conceptualized as environmental stimuli; flow experience, perceived trust, and perceived risk thought of as biological events; and the physical reaction is buy intention. The level of virtuality is introduced as a moderating boundary condition. Data were collected from 1,061 valid questionnaires obtained through a multi-channel survey, including 552 respondents upper-anthropomorphism collective 509 in the low-anthropomorphism team. The sample was relatively balanced in gender and primarily composed of young consumers aged 18–25. Multi-group The suggested ties were tested using a model of structural equations. The conclusions drawn reveal three key findings. First, attractiveness and interactivity directly influence purchase intention only under high-virtuality conditions, highlighting the contingent nature of these effects. Second, flow experience and perceived trust function as positive mediators linking virtual anchor characteristics to purchase intention. Third, contrary to conventional expectations, greater attractiveness and interactivity increase perceived risk, and this paradoxical effect is amplified under high levels of virtuality. Additionally, virtuality significantly moderates most mediating pathways. These findings extend SOR literature by identifying virtuality as a critical boundary condition in human–AI interaction and revealing a risk-enhancing mechanism of appealing AI anchors. Practically, the results provide actionable insights for platform designers and marketers regarding the strategic deployment of virtual anchors based on anthropomorphic realism.

detail.title: Research on the Design and Development of Construction Toy for Children Aged 4–6 Based on AHP-QFD
detail.abstract: This study developed "Little Explorer," a construction toy for children aged 4–6, aiming to support cognitive development while serving educational and companion roles. Using design-development research, a prototype underwent iterative refinement and multi-stage user testing. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) established user requirement weights, which guided optimization via Quality Function Deployment (QFD). Evaluation results demonstrated that the final design significantly outperformed the initial prototype in cognitive enhancement, child engagement, and operational flexibility. These findings confirm the toy successfully meets young children's needs for an interactive, instructive, and enjoyable building experience, effectively blending learning with play.

detail.abstract: Long form podcast-style conversations featuring film actors, directors, and influential hosts are increasingly used as high-commitment promotional touchpoints that can shape what audiences watch, when they watch, and where they watch, yet research and practice still lack a clear process model that explains how sustained listening translates into downstream market outcomes. This paper develops a conceptual Antecedents, Decision, Outcomes framework for film-marketing in the attention economy by treating listening as an active allocation of scarce attention, specifying parasocial engagement and perceived source credibility as the central conversion mechanisms, and identifying key antecedents including audience motives, individual dispositions, and platform affordances such as discovery and accessibility. The model theorizes outcomes beyond simple intention, including timing and venue choice, word of mouth, social sharing, and loyalty loops that extend engagement across films, stars, genres, hosts, and platforms. By reframing long form conversations as strategic attention infrastructure rather than peripheral publicity, the paper offers testable propositions and actionable implications for marketers, platforms, and filmmakers seeking to design long form appearances that convert visibility into commitment.

detail.abstract: On 6 February 2023, the Kahramanmaraş-centered earthquakes reduced large parts of southern Türkiye to rubble. Countless buildings collapsed or became uninhabitable. Yet one public building remained standing: the Adıyaman Provincial Public Library. Amid the devastation, this fact was impossible to ignore. This observation became the starting point of my master’s thesis, which examined the earthquake risk of public libraries in Türkiye using Geographic Information Systems (GIS). It also raised a more immediate and human question: what can a library that remains standing actually do after a disaster?

detail.abstract: In modern societies, many of the hardest problems are not “single-point” problems. They are system problems. A rumor jumps across communities in hours. A public service reaches some groups quickly but misses others. Platform risks reappear in new forms even after repeated governance actions. In education, healthcare, and emergency management, we have plenty of data—yet decision-makers still struggle to pinpoint which connections, pathways, and bottlenecks truly drive outcomes. What is missing is often not data, but a way to represent multi-actor, multi-relationship, and multi-context complexity in a form that computers can learn from and humans can interpret. This is where heterogeneous graphs come in.

title: Static Rules for Dynamic Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Static Rules for Dynamic Systems
detail.abstract: The EU AI Act represents the most comprehensive binding attempt to regulate artificial intelligence to date. Its risk-based framework, conformity assessment obligations, and transparency requirements reflect a serious effort to bring AI development under meaningful legal oversight. Yet the Act rests on a foundational assumption that is increasingly difficult to sustain: that AI systems can be meaningfully evaluated at a fixed point in time and that compliance established at deployment will remain valid across a system's operational life. This assumption was plausible for early generations of AI systems with narrow, well-defined functions. It is increasingly implausible for the systems now entering deployment: foundation models that underpin diverse downstream applications, agentic systems that learn from interaction, and multi-model pipelines where emergent behaviour arises from the interaction of components no single actor controls. For these systems, a compliance snapshot taken at market placement may accurately describe the system as it existed on the day of assessment while saying very little about how it will behave six months later. The core governance gap is not opacity-it is adaptivity. A system may be fully transparent at time T and yet behave in ways its developers did not anticipate at time T+n. Static certification frameworks are structurally unable to address this.

title: The Governance Mismatch: Why Traditional IT Governance Produces the Behavior It Is Supposed to Prevent
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Governance Mismatch: Why Traditional IT Governance Produces the Behavior It Is Supposed to Prevent
detail.abstract: Enterprise IT governance frameworks continue to operate through centralized permission, committee review, and approval-based control even as the organizations they govern have moved to continuous delivery, distributed architectures, and cloud-native infrastructure. The mismatch between governance design and operating reality is evident in most mature technology organizations, where governance processes are both extensive and ineffective: policies are documented, committees convene, approvals accumulate, yet the most consequential failures occur within the governance envelope rather than outside it. This paper argues that the mismatch is not incidental. It is what you get when governance designs built for centralized, slow-moving, predictable environments are retrofitted onto operating environments that no longer have those properties. Drawing on behavioral science, sociology, and systems thinking, the paper argues that governance is a behavioral system. It produces the behaviors it incentivizes. Under modern conditions, permission-based governance systematically incentivizes the behaviors it is designed to prevent: concealment of risk, optimization for approval over correctness, shadow governance, workarounds, and disengagement. Five design principles are proposed as a starting framework for constraint-based IT governance. Encoded constraints replace permissions. Persistent ownership replaces role assignment. Evidence produced by the work replaces documentation produced separately. Metrics as inquiry replace metrics as targets. Defaults that hold under stress replace policy-dependent compliance. None of this is presented as a proven model. It is a starting point for a conversation about how governance design might be brought into alignment with the operating reality it claims to govern. The paper offers no empirical validation and does not claim to have solved the governance problem. It argues only that the behavioral sciences have something useful to say about why current governance fails, and that the conversation about what should replace it is one worth having.

title: TRUMP Memecoin: Promotional Events, Supply Concentration, and Investor Outcomes
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: TRUMP Memecoin: Promotional Events, Supply Concentration, and Investor Outcomes
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the Trump memecoin, a Solana-based token launched on January 18, 2025. Using publicly available price data from Yahoo Finance and on-chain reports from blockchain analytics firms, this study documents three key findings. First, the token experienced a 93.4% decline from its all-time closing price high of $45.50 on January 19, 2025, to $3.00 on March 27, 2026. Second, two exclusive promotional events hosted by Trump-affiliated entities, a May 2025 dinner at Trump National Golf Club and an announced April 2026 gala at Mar-a-Lago, created temporary price spikes but did not reverse the long-term downward trend. Third, approximately 80% of the token supply is controlled by Trump-affiliated entities, raising ethical concerns about the alignment of promotional activities with retail investor protection. These findings extend prior research on political memecoins and speculative financial assets.

title: Inference on Indirect Effects in Spatial Econometric Models
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Geography and Resource Management

detail.title: Inference on Indirect Effects in Spatial Econometric Models
detail.abstract: Standard confidence intervals for indirect effects in spatial autoregressive models treat the estimated spatial parameter ρ as known. This article shows that this plugin procedure can produce 95% confidence intervals whose actual coverage is as low as 26%, with a median of 53% across configurations, because the indirect effect multiplier is one to two orders of magnitude more sensitive to perturbations in ρ than the direct effect multiplier. A classification result establishes that models with ρ in the conditional mean (SAR, SDM) require correction, while models with it only in the error distribution (SEM, SDEM) do not. A closed-form variance formula is derived for a marginalized test statistic that integrates over profile likelihood weights. Monte Carlo experiments across 48 configurations confirm that the correction restores rejection rates to 4.2-6.3% and coverage to 96-97%. The plug-in method controls size but not coverage, and the delta method achieves adequate coverage but has approximately zero power under the null. Among the methods examined, only the proposed correction achieves both correct size and adequate coverage.

title: Governance-by-Design for Trustworthy LLMs: A Neurosymbolic Architectural Framework
affiliations: Hellenic Open University, Hellenic Open University, Hellenic Open University, University of Piraeus and Hellenic Open University

detail.title: Governance-by-Design for Trustworthy LLMs: A Neurosymbolic Architectural Framework

declarations.funderStatement: This work has been supported by the Pandora European Horizon project (Grant Agreement No 101135775)

detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong empirical performance across a wide range of information-processing and decision-support tasks, yet their deployment in high-stakes socio-technical systems remains problematic due to limited controllability, lack of explicit accountability and susceptibility to hallucination and non-deterministic behaviour. This paper argues that such limitations cannot be addressed through model-centric techniques alone but require governance mechanisms to be embedded at the level of system architecture. We introduce a governance-by-design neurosymbolic architecture that enforces trustworthiness as an invariant system property rather than an emergent outcome of model behaviour. The proposed framework structures information flow across four architectural layers-data-proximal processing, symbolic grounding and analytical reasoning, coordination and control, and user-facing interaction-while confining language models to bounded and temporally restricted roles. From an implementation perspective, we describe the instantiation of the system that translates these architectural principles into executable constraints and empirically validate key trustworthiness properties, including evidence-bounded generation, conservative failure, provenance completeness and reproducibility, among others. The results demonstrate that accountability, governance and control can be enforced by design through the proposed neurosymbolic system architecture, thus providing a principled foundation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in regulated and high-stakes environments.

title: Bargaining Inefficiencies and a Solution using Preliminary Contracts

detail.title: Bargaining Inefficiencies and a Solution using Preliminary Contracts
detail.abstract: The basic model of this paper analyzes seller-buyer bargaining games where players have fixed bargaining costs and may also discount the future. Players can terminate bargaining in any period. If there are finite periods or after a certain number of periods, only one player can make offers, players terminate bargaining without a single offer made. If there are infinite periods and bilateral offers, players may take too long to reach a deal. My alternative model fixes these inefficiencies. In the alternative model, offers are made simultaneously and each player can make only one offer. A deal happens when at least one of the offers is not rejected by the other player.

title: Sectoral Macroprudential Policy and the Sectoral Allocation of Bank Credit

detail.title: Sectoral Macroprudential Policy and the Sectoral Allocation of Bank Credit

declarations.funderStatement: Fundación Ramón Areces

detail.abstract: A novel credit dataset for 72 countries has been constructed. It contains bank credit disaggregated by borrowing sector. I show that household-targeted macroprudential policy not only reduces credit to households but also, via spillover effects, increases credit to firms. By virtue of these effects, the share of corporate credit in banks' loan portfolios increases. These results entail that sectoral macroprudential policy can influence the sectoral allocation of bank credit. It is shown that borrower-based household-targeted macroprudential policy tools, as opposed to lender-based tools, have the strongest bearing on banks' sectoral allocation of credit. Additionaly, household-targeted macroprudential policy tools are found to reduce the nonperforming loans ratio.

title: Information Aggregation with AI Agents
affiliations: Durham University

detail.title: Information Aggregation with AI Agents

declarations.funderStatement: This research is based on work funded under ESRC grant ES/V004425/1.

detail.abstract: Can Large Language Models (AI agents) aggregate dispersed private information through trading and reason about the knowledge of others by observing price movements? We conduct a controlled experiment where AI agents trade in a prediction market after receiving private signals, measuring information aggregation by the log error of the last price. We find that although the median market is effective at aggregating information in the easy information structures, increasing the complexity has a significant and negative impact, suggesting that AI agents suffer from the same limitations as humans when reasoning about others. Consistent with our theoretical predictions, information aggregation remains unaffected by allowing cheap talk communication, changing the duration of the market or initial price, and strategic prompting-thus demonstrating that prediction markets are robust. We establish that "smarter" AI agents perform better at aggregation and they are more profitable. Surprisingly, giving them feedback about past performance makes them worse at aggregation and reduces their profits.

title: What Text Helps Forecast Inflation? Evidence from Retrieval-augmented Language Models
affiliations: and Kristiania University College

detail.title: What Text Helps Forecast Inflation? Evidence from Retrieval-augmented Language Models
detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly explored in macroeconomic forecasting. They can process rich qualitative information, including central bank communications and financial news narratives, that standard econometric models cannot easily incorporate. Retrieval-augmented generation extends this capability by grounding the model in up-to-date documents retrieved at the time of forecasting, overcoming the staleness of knowledge encoded in fixed model parameters. Building on these two ideas, we develop a RAG-based pipeline to forecast U.S. CPI inflation at horizons of one to twelve months. The system retrieves and filters passages from central bank communications and financial news, and integrates them with numeric historical CPI data through structured prompting. On a genuinely outof-sample evaluation window, the best RAG-augmented configuration outperforms conventional econometric benchmarks, with gains concentrated at longer horizons where traditional time-series models struggle most. Source-level analysis reveals that different textual domains contribute unevenly across horizons: Central bank communications anchor short-run forecasts, while news content contributes more at longer horizons. Text augmentation also improves density forecast calibration, shifting prediction intervals from severe overconfidence toward near-nominal coverage. However, not all retrieved content is beneficial. A topic-channel analysis shows that demand-and energy-related text improves forecasts, whereas monetary policy content is consistently harmful.

detail.title: Inequitable Sentencing Disparities in Insider Trading

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 732
publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Sentencing disparities prevail in the insider trading criminal context. On average, corporate directors and officers convicted of insider trading are treated significantly more lenient than rank-and-file employees as well as other offenders convicted of the same offense. These disparities exist even though these high-level executives profit millions more on average than their lower-level insider counterparts. This phenomenon exists in direct contradiction to the Sentencing Guidelines. Faithful implementation of these Guidelines would result in such high-level offenders receiving criminal sentences that would be substantially more severe than currently is the situation.

The purpose of this Article is to examine the causes, symptoms, and reach of this phenomenon, and to propose mitigating solutions. Through anecdotal and empirical analyses, this Article ascertains the sheer depth and breadth of insider trading sentencing disparities. This Article reviews the legally salient facts and circumstances of dozens of high-profile and undeservedly low-profile insider-trading cases and questions the normative propriety of the resultant prison sentences. Additionally, this Article aggregates sentencing data from over one-hundred recent criminal cases to assess from a broader perspective patterns and inequities across the insider trading sentencing landscape. This cogitation of micro-level and macro-level analyses shows that the application of the Sentencing Guidelines, when combined with routine departure from these Guidelines by federal judges, has culminated in an inequitable sentencing regime with respect to insider trading offenders. To ameliorate this situation, this Article proposes deemphasizing financial harm-based sentencing enhancements to prioritize a more important measurement of culpability – namely, fiduciary breach.

detail.abstract: Corporate diversity efforts in the United States are widely perceived to be in retreat. This chapter argues that this perception misstates the legal reality. This chapter offers a governance-based framework for navigating this environment.

detail.abstract:
Do banks fail because of runs or because they become insolvent? Answering this question is central to understanding financial crises and designing effective financial stability policies. Long-run historical evidence reveals that the root cause of bank failures is usually insolvency. The importance of bank runs is somewhat overstated. Runs matter, but in most cases they trigger or accelerate failure at already weak banks, rather than cause otherwise sound banks to fail.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Monetary Policy: A Framework and Perspective on Cyclical Transmission, Structural Transition, and Financial Stability

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Monetary Policy: A Framework and Perspective on Cyclical Transmission, Structural Transition, and Financial Stability

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1192
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: I develop a framework analyzing how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes monetary policy through three interrelated channels: cyclical transmission, structural transition, and financial stability. In the short run, AI can alter inflation dynamics by changing how supply and demand disturbances map into pricesthrough shifts in production technologies, pricing behavior, cost pass-through, and expectations-even when conventional measures of economic slack are unchanged. Over longer horizons, AI may shift the natural benchmarks around which policy is calibrated, including potential output and the natural rate of interest. For financial stability, AI may improve credit allocation and risk assessment, but can also heighten systemic vulnerabilities through inflated expectation-driven asset valuations and model monocultures. A particular risk arises at the intersection of these channels: if AI initially depresses realized efficiency through adoption frictions while simultaneously fueling elevated asset valuations, the economy may face cost-push inflation and financial fragility at once-an AI-specific stagflation risk that the interest rate instrument alone is ill-suited to address. I argue that AI does not call for a redefinition of central banks' objectives, but it does require a recalibration of existing frameworks: its diffusion blurs the distinction between cyclical fluctuations and structural shifts, raising the value of cost-side diagnostics and robust policy strategies over exclusive reliance on reduced-form inflation-gap relationships.

title: Motherhood and Violence

detail.title: Motherhood and Violence
detail.abstract: Two factors shape women's exposure to intimate partner violence (IPV): whether partners use violence and whether women remain in violent relationships. Standard IPV measures cannot separate these margins, yet they imply different policy responses. I propose a framework to disentangle them in the context of motherhood, when IPV exposure often rises. A simple model yields distinct predictions which can be tested with data recording past violence and separation histories. Using Mexican survey data with these features and exogenous fertility variation from pharmacy openings, I find that motherhood increases violence exposure entirely through reduced exit, not changes in men's behavior.

title: Bulgaria 2126: A Model of State Viability Under a Deficit of Continuity

detail.title: Bulgaria 2126: A Model of State Viability Under a Deficit of Continuity

detail.abstract:
This independent analytical paper introduces a structured diagnostic framework for long-term state viability under conditions of demographic contraction and chronic political instability. Bulgaria is examined through five interdependent systems — demography, productivity, territory, state capacity, and external integration — linked by causal chains and feedback loops.  

A simplified illustrative Continuity Index (CI) is proposed as a diagnostic proxy to approximate policy persistence across electoral cycles. An indicative estimate for 2021–2026 places Bulgaria in the 35–45% range, near the threshold where negative feedback loops begin to dominate. Four scenarios to 2126 are developed, with the critical window identified as 2026–2035 following Eurozone accession.  

The framework treats continuity not as a secondary political issue, but as the central operating condition determining whether structural decline becomes self-reinforcing or reversible. It is designed as a practical diagnostic tool for policy discussion and long-term foresight rather than as an econometrically validated index.

title: From Commodity Volatility to Public Wealth: Reserve Adequacy, Fiscal Rules, and Sequenced SWF Design in Mongolia

detail.title: From Commodity Volatility to Public Wealth: Reserve Adequacy, Fiscal Rules, and Sequenced SWF Design in Mongolia

declarations.ethicsApproval: The views expressed in this paper are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the official position of The Bank of Mongolia.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Resource-dependent economies face persistent macroeconomic volatility arising from commodity price fluctuations, fiscal pro-cyclicality, and external vulnerability. While these conditions strengthen the economic rationale for sovereign wealth funds (SWFs), they also complicate fund design in settings characterized by evolving institutional capacity and fiscal constraints. This paper develops a readiness-based macroeconomic diagnostic framework for SWF design that explicitly links macroeconomic risk, objective hierarchy, governance feasibility, and mandate sequencing within a policy-oriented modelling structure. The framework is empirically illustrated using quarterly macroeconomic data for Mongolia over the period 2017Q1–2025Q3, with a focus on the Future Heritage Fund as a public wealth management institution. The empirical diagnostics indicate that Mongolia exhibits high commodity-linked volatility, a structural public savings constraint, and an intergenerational wealth challenge associated with exhaustible natural resource revenues. Consistent with the model’s diagnostic dominance and feasibility conditions, a long-horizon, savings-oriented SWF—anchored by conservative early-stage investment mandates and rule-based fiscal integration—emerges as the most coherent and sustainable design. By framing SWF design as a constrained feasibility problem rather than a portfolio optimization exercise, the paper contributes a modelling-based approach for aligning macroeconomic stability objectives, governance capacity, and mandate sequencing. Beyond the Mongolia case, the framework provides policy-relevant analytical guidance for Asian resource-dependent economies seeking to strengthen macroeconomic and financial stability, fiscal governance, and long-term public wealth management under conditions of commodity-driven volatility.

title: Weapons, Wealth, and the Fates of Societies
affiliations: , Columbia University and

detail.title: Weapons, Wealth, and the Fates of Societies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors have nothing to disclose
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Why do weapons sustain durable peace in some societies but provoke perpetual violence in others? We develop a theory in which the value of human life and the frequency of violence are jointly determined by weapons technology and economic conditions. Lethal weapons deter conflict but raise mortality, taxing the future returns to investing in one's livelihood. When those returns are high, deterrence dominates: peace and investment reinforce each other. When those returns are low, the mortality tax dominates: agents divest from the future, the value of life falls, and violence deepens-a trap that deadlier weapons worsen. Whether weapons pacify or destabilize depends on the interaction between their offensive characteristics and the baseline prosperity of the society they enter. The theory explains four historical puzzles: why Tokugawa Japan (1603-1868), having mastered firearms, abandoned them and gained two centuries of peace and prosperity; why firearms traded into West Africa and among Native American nations (17th-18th century) produced escalating violence and persistent underdevelopment rather than deterrence; how Iceland (930-1262) sustained stateless order without a sovereign; and why Rome's late Republic descended into civil war as military reforms created a landless soldiery with no livelihood to protect and imperial plunder to fight over. The model also refines the logic of nuclear deterrence and generates testable predictions about urban gun violence in high-poverty neighborhoods.

title: Equity Auctions with Bidder Moral Hazard
affiliations: Nanjing University, University of Western Ontario and Nanjing University

detail.title: Equity Auctions with Bidder Moral Hazard
detail.abstract: This study considers standard equity auctions in the presence of winner's postauction effort as bidder moral hazard. The valuation of the auctioned object is endogenously determined by the winner's effort and private type. We characterize the equilibria of the first-price equity auction (FPEA) and the second-price equity auction (SPEA) under various environments with bidder moral hazard. Regarding performance comparison, we identify the conditions under which the FPEA features, in equilibrium, a lower equity share payment, higher total surplus, equal bidder payoffs, and a higher seller payoff in expectation. Consequently, the FPEA Pareto dominates the SPEA in terms of expected bidder and seller payoffs. We further identify the conditions under which bidder payoff equivalence does not hold while the FPEA maintains an advantage in the expected total surplus and the expected seller payoff. Lastly, we compare equity auctions with fixed-royalty auctions under bidder moral hazard and investigate equity auctions under double moral hazard.

detail.abstract: Design/methodology/approach-We conducted an online questionnaire survey using a discrete choice experiment (DCE) to test our hypotheses. The sample size was 446 from Japan and 195 from Thailand, and we set four attributes: price,brand,country of origin from hill tribes, and fair trade label. An orthogonal design was generated with the AlgDesign package in R. Findings-This study revealed that ethical cues have different effects in different cultures. It may depend on the Thai-specific meaning and recognition of "Hill Tribe" and the setting of the price range. This study found that trust transfer and signal integrity frameworks exhibit strong dependence on cultural and market context. Practical implications-We suggests that managers and other actors who communicate ethical information should tailor the use of ethical cues to the target market. Specifically, while an integrated presentation of multiple cues may be effective in Japan, in Thailand communicators should carefully assess the semantic congruence among ethical cues and instead prioritize a clear, single signal, complemented by consumer education. Originality/value-This paper offers cross-cultural evidence on whether multiple ethical/quality cues function as complements or substitutes and quantifies willingness-to-pay (WTP) differences between Japanese and Thai consumers in a realistic multi-cue choice context.

detail.abstract: The objective of this study is to examine the effect of corruption on non-performing loans in 17 Central and Eastern European countries from 2004 to 2021. The study investigates the influence of corruption on the incidence of non-performing loans while controlling for macroeconomic, bank-specific, and governance-related factors. The analysis is based on panel data, and the fixed effects method is applied. The results indicate that several variables, including corruption, unemployment, loan-to-deposit ratio, voice and accountability index, and credit growth significantly affect non-performing loans. The findings contribute to the existing literature by examining the role of external factors in the persistence of non-performing loans, revisiting this issue in the specific context of the Central and Eastern European region.

detail.abstract: Despite unprecedented investment in Insurance Technology (InsurTech), the boundary of insurability continues to shrink rather than expand. This paradox suggests that current innovations prioritize technical efficiency while neglecting deeper institutional reconstruction. This paper proposes a novel analytical framework, the S-R-C-I Institutional Innovation Navigation System, to diagnose and navigate this dilemma. Grounded in New Institutional Economics (Coase, Williamson) and operationalizing Munger's "3T" transaction cost framework, this study redefines InsurTech not as technological application, but as the strategic reconstruction of interactions between Risk (S), Resilience Resources (R), Capital Allocation Mechanisms (C), and Penetrative Information (I).

detail.abstract: The study investigates the determinants of bank non-performing loans (NPL) in European and African countries, focusing on 32 European and African countries from 2010 to 2021. The results based on the two-stage least squares regression methodology show that the number of commercial bank branch, bank liquid reserves to bank assets ratio, inflation rate, exchange rate, real interest rate and the lending rate are significant determinants of bank NPL in the full sample. Size of domestic private credit, bank capital to asset ratio, bank liquid reserve to bank asset ratio, unemployment rate, inflation rate, exchange rate, real interest rate and lending rate are significant determinants of bank NPL in European countries. Bank capital to asset ratio, bank liquid reserve to bank asset ratio and inflation rate in Africa are significant determinants of bank NPL in African countries. The implication of the results is that the determinants of bank NPL in European countries are not necessarily the drivers of bank NPL in African countries.

detail.abstract: Financial inclusion entails ownership of a formal account, such as a bank account, Fintech account or mobile money account, which can be used to access basic financial services and to send or receive digital payments. This essay analyses the global and regional trends in financial inclusion of the older population. A descriptive analysis of the World Bank Global Findex 2021 micro-data for the older age group was conducted. The findings reveal that financial inclusion of older adults, in terms of formal account ownership of any type, is greater in high-income OECD countries (98%), North America (96%) and the Euro Area (99%). In contrast, financial inclusion of older adults is much lower in low-income countries (25%), the Arab world (44%), sub-Saharan Africa (44%), and Middle East and North African (MENA) countries (57%). There is disproportionate progress in financial inclusion of older people across regions particularly in the 'financial institution account' and 'use of digital payments' categories. This disparity calls for more coordinated effort to expand access to financial services for older adults and ensure that they have access to old-age-appropriate credit, savings, payment and insurance products that enable them to live a meaningful life even in old age. Notable challenges to financial inclusion of the aging population include low income, discrimination, and poor formal saving culture. However, policymakers can address these challenges by encouraging financial service providers to offer tailored financial products, provide financial education and awareness, introduce digital literacy programs, and increase financial capability of older adults.

title: Climate Hazards, Childhood Experiences, and Development Trajectories: The Long-Term Impact of GLOF Exposure

detail.title: Climate Hazards, Childhood Experiences, and Development Trajectories: The Long-Term Impact of GLOF Exposure
detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term impact of childhood exposure to Glacier Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) on adult human capital in High Mountain Asia. Using historical GLOF data and geospatial mapping, we identify treatment and control groups based on geographic proximity. Exposed children attain 1.4–1.7 fewer years of schooling and have 1.9–2.2 kg/m2 lower adultBMI. Rural adolescents face greater educational losses, whereas urban residents experience more pronounced health impacts. Our ﬁndings highlight the long-term costs of climate-induced disasters and underscore the need for targeted risk reduction in vulnerable mountain communities.

detail.title: AGL Loss: Optimizing Binary Classification by Asymmetric Generalized Logarithmic Loss Function with Statistical Validation

contentType.other: It is submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems and is under review.

publicationDetails.detailsText: It is submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems and is under review

detail.abstract: Robust and stable binary classification forms the foundation of numerous real-world applications, including medical diagnostics and autonomous systems. However, models trained with the widely used Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss often suffer from instability, high variance, and inconsistent optimization, particularly under noisy, imbalanced, and heterogeneous data conditions. To address these challenges, we reformulate BCE as the Asymmetric Generalized Logarithmic (AGL) loss, which unifies both label cases in a single logarithmic term while preserving convexity and O(1) complexity. AGL integrates a stabilized logarithmic formulation with parameterized control, enabling smoother training dynamics and mitigating loss spikes during the training, where BCE typically fails. Through theoretical analysis, we show that AGL gradients match BCE magnitudes exactly for both labels, while Hessian scaling is smoother near boundaries. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that AGL achieves up to ≈ 42% lower cumulative training loss. Crucially, AGL exhibits superior asymptotic stability, reducing late-stage volatility by 9 orders of magnitude (σAGL ≈ 10^-12 vs σBCE ≈ 10^-3) compared to BCE. In noisy and unbalanced scenarios, AGL shows improved stability and competitive performance, with significant gains in high-noise regimes. These findings establish AGL as a robust and practical alternative to BCE, particularly in resource-constrained environments where training stability and efficiency are critical.

title: Information Choice and Shock Transmission
affiliations: University of Alberta

detail.title: Information Choice and Shock Transmission
detail.abstract: The paper proposes an information-based theory of shock transmission which explains how the impact of a shock can decrease with exposure to it. I develop a model in which decision-makers learn about the risk factors they are exposed to, but have limited capacity to process information. I find that decision-makers optimally learn more about the risk factors they are more exposed to, which enables them to mitigate the direct impact of shocks by minimizing the loss due to suboptimal action. On the other hand, the impact of shocks to risk factors that they are relatively less exposed to is amplified through their poorly informed decision-making.

title: Cross Border Mergers and Acquisitions Under Indian Law: Regulatory Framework, Challenges, and Future Prospects

detail.title: Cross Border Mergers and Acquisitions Under Indian Law: Regulatory Framework, Challenges, and Future Prospects
detail.abstract:
The research examines how cross-border mergers and acquisitions operate under Indian corporate law. Companies now conduct international restructuring activities international trade and foreign investments have expanded their business operations outside their home countries. The study investigates the legal frameworks which regulate these mergers through the Companies Act of 2013 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act of 1999 and the associated rules which the Reserve Bank of India has established.

The paper further provides an assessment of how regulatory organizations like the National Company Law Tribunal and the Competition Commission of India participate in the process of cross-border transactions approvals. It also highlights practical challenges including procedural delays, regulatory overlaps, taxation concerns, and valuation issues. The study demonstrates that India has established a legal system which allows cross-border mergers to occur, yet the country requires specific reforms to enhance operational processes and support international business expansions.

title: Synchronizing Global Alliances: From Diplomatic Protocols to Executional Drivers A Framework for Institutionalizing Strategic International Cooperation

detail.title: Synchronizing Global Alliances: From Diplomatic Protocols to Executional Drivers A Framework for Institutionalizing Strategic International Cooperation
detail.abstract: This research addresses the "execution gap" within international cooperation. Based on years of close observation in diplomatic environments, it argues that the proliferation of Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) has led to an "intent inflation" that lacks operational sustainability. This paper proposes a transition from "Paper Diplomacy" to "Executive Diplomacy" through a tripartite framework: Structuring Project Processing Units (PPUs), enhancing Cultural Intelligence (CQ) as a de-risking tool, and aligning all global activities with sovereign strategic goals, specifically using Saudi Vision 2030 as a primary model for success.

title: Environmental Misinformation and Housing Prices
affiliations: HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong and Hunan University - School of Economics and Trade

detail.title: Environmental Misinformation and Housing Prices
detail.abstract: This paper studies how environmental misinformation distorts housing prices and how real environmental events affect the distortion. Using transaction-level data on China’s pre-sale housing market, we examine a persistent “dust-floor” rumor, which claims that apartments on floors 9 to 11 of a building have higher exposure to particulate matter pollution. Our identification leverages exogenous variation in air quality, combined with a shock on buyers’ attention to the rumor led by a developer liquidity crisis, and comparison between rumor affected floors and neighboring floors. We find that the misinformation lowers housing prices by 1.8% during non-sandstorm seasons and 5.3% during sandstorm seasons, comparable to half of the price impact of real environmental information from the Toxic Release Inventory disclosure. The price penalty is partially driven by reallocation of demands across nearby real-estate projects and towards cheaper housings.

title: Optimal Size and Composition of Government Spending in Small Open Economies
affiliations: Monash University, Queensland University of Technology, Monash University and Australian National University (ANU)

detail.title: Optimal Size and Composition of Government Spending in Small Open Economies
detail.abstract: We study optimal ﬁscal policy over the business cycle in a small open economy within a currency union that faces downward nominal wage rigidity. Government spending consists of public consumption and productive public investment, with investment accumulating into public capital subject to a time-to-build requirement. In this environment, we characterize the Ramsey allocation when the policymaker jointly chooses consumption taxes, public consumption, and public investment. Fiscal instruments operate through distinct but complementary margins. The consumption tax mitigates unemployment distortions when wage rigidity binds, while spending composition provides an additional intertemporal stabilization margin. Because public capital is subject to time-to-build and has limited short-run elasticity, counter-cyclical public investment smooths private consumption and stabilizes relative prices with modest contemporaneous distortions. Calibrating the model to France, we ﬁnd that coordinated ﬁscal policy substantially reduces unemployment risk and generates measurable welfare gains relative to regimes that rely solely on taxes or keep government spending composition ﬁxed. These results are robust to alternative calibrations and to an extension with government production of non-tradable public goods.

title: The URIL-Flux Equation: A Unified Dynamical Framework for Urban-Rural Factor Mobility

detail.title: The URIL-Flux Equation: A Unified Dynamical Framework for Urban-Rural Factor Mobility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study uses anonymous, minimal-risk survey data. Participation was voluntary and no personally identifiable information was collected. No formal ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the URIL-Flux equation, a unified dynamical formulation of urban–rural factor mobility under institutional friction. The framework specifies realized mobility (Φ) as a multiplicative function of individual kinetic capacity (σ) and structural potential gradient (∇Ψ), attenuated exponentially by institutionally mediated resistance scaled by heterogeneous adaptive capacity (λ): Φ = σ · ∇Ψ · e^(−λR). The model integrates structural opportunity differentials, individual mobilization capacity, and institutional damping within a single computable functional form. The exponential structure implies nonlinear attenuation, heterogeneous sensitivity to institutional friction, and regime-dependent mobility realization. An illustrative pilot implementation demonstrates the operationalizability of the framework through structured index construction and log-linear approximation. The empirical exercise is exploratory and intended to validate feasibility rather than establish definitive parameter estimates. The primary contribution lies in formalizing an integrative and falsifiable representation of mobility dynamics that connects micro-level agency with macro-level structural gradients through explicit attenuation mechanics. This paper constitutes the first formal public disclosure of the URIL-Flux functional structure.

title: Land Rights Awareness and Community Engagement in Resource Management: Evidence from a Lab-in-the-Field Experiment in Liberia
affiliations: Oregon State University and Oregon State University

detail.title: Land Rights Awareness and Community Engagement in Resource Management: Evidence from a Lab-in-the-Field Experiment in Liberia
detail.abstract: Effective management of common-pool resources is critical for sustainable development in lowincome settings, where formal enforcement capacity is often limited. We use a lab-in-the-field experiment in Liberia to study how peer communication and legal-rights information shape individual tree extraction decisions. Our legal information treatments provide a structured summary of key provisions of Liberia’s Land Rights Act, while a facilitated treatment supplements this summary with guided explanation and a question-and-answer session to deepen comprehension. Relative to an open-access baseline, both peer communication and basic legal information reduce tree harvesting by 22–26%, and the facilitated legal information treatment decreases extraction by 30%. Introducing a simulated resource collapse before any intervention increases harvesting by 9% relative to open access, consistent with panic-driven over-extraction under uncertainty. In contrast, when the same shock follows the interventions, harvesting falls by 5%. Linking game behavior to detailed pre-intervention household characteristics shows that baseline extraction closely mirrors real-world resource-use incentives, indicating that the experiment captures meaningful, not artificial, decision making. These findings show that combining local deliberation with a strengthened understanding of property rights can curb over-extraction and promote cooperative responses to scarcity, even in the absence of strong formal enforcement. More broadly, these results highlight the value of legally grounded information and community engagement in fostering self-sustaining resource governance in developing-country contexts.

title: Economic Evaluation of Whole Genome Sequencing Guided Treatment for Rifampicin-Resistant Tuberculosis: A Within-Trial Analysis of the SMARTT Trial

detail.title: Economic Evaluation of Whole Genome Sequencing Guided Treatment for Rifampicin-Resistant Tuberculosis: A Within-Trial Analysis of the SMARTT Trial

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None of the authors declare a competing interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The trial and health economic analysis were approved by the ethics committees of the Free State University, Stellenbosch University, and the University of Antwerp. All participants gave written informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Research Foundation Flanders (FWO) under TBM grant N° T001018N and Odysseus grant N° G0F8316N.

detail.abstract:
Background: Whole genome sequencing (WGS) can guide effective rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) treatment but the cost is a perceived barrier.

Methods: We performed a health-economic evaluation of culture-based WGS combined with automated recommendation for an all-oral 6-month individualized regimen. Provider, patient and household costs for RR-TB management were analyzed for 203 participants randomized to the WGS intervention or standard of care (SOC) in the South African SMARTT trial (Sept 2021-Feb 2023). Cost-effectiveness was assessed by incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER); monetary value by Incremental Net Monetary Benefit (INMB) and Return on Investment (ROI).

Findings: WGS-guided treatment was dominant, reducing the per patient mean total cost (-$370) and increasing the per patient health benefit (-0.05 DALYs), resulting in an INMB of $618. Society gained $3.61 for every dollar invested. Among people living with HIV, WGS-guided treatment resulted in greater cost reduction (-$582 vs -$22), greater DALY reduction (-0.08 vs -0.01) and higher INMB ($969 vs $51). The benefit was larger for women than men (cost savings $694 vs $191, DALY reduction -0.06 vs -0.03, and INMBs $997 vs $319). People with expanded resistance experienced the greatest health benefit (0.46 DALYs averted), but the intervention was not cost-effective in this population (INMB $-1231) due to higher drug ($1690 vs $1260) and inpatient costs ($4,244 vs $1,201).

Interpretation: WGS-guided RR-TB treatment was cost-effective and society gained $3.6 benefit for every dollar invested. Future research should evaluate the cost-effectiveness of WGS-guided treatment in contexts where an all-oral 6-month regimen is the SOC.

title: Internal Security Governance: A Case Study of Inter-Agency Coordination in India

detail.title: Internal Security Governance: A Case Study of Inter-Agency Coordination in India
detail.abstract: This research examines the complexities of inter-agency coordination within India's internal security framework. As threats evolve into hybrid and transnational forms, the efficiency of bureaucratic and operational synergy between central ministries and state-level agencies becomes critical. Utilizing a case-study methodology informed by practitioner insights at the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), this paper analyzes the structural bottlenecks that hinder seamless data sharing and resource mobilization. The study focuses on the "silo effect" within traditional administrative hierarchies and evaluates the impact of recent digital governance initiatives on real-time response capabilities. By bridging the gap between management theory and political science, the research proposes a streamlined "Integrated Governance Model" to enhance institutional resilience. This paper provides essential perspectives for policymakers and scholars aiming to optimize internal security architectures in complex federal democracies.

title: Between Agent and Governor: Local Officials' Selective Implementation of Religious Policies in China

detail.title: Between Agent and Governor: Local Officials' Selective Implementation of Religious Policies in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research is done with approval from the Committee for Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS),protocol number: 2017-05-9967.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the National Science Foundation [#1747183], the Global Religion Research Initiative at the University of Notre Dame, and the University of California, Berkeley.

detail.abstract: Under the "decentralized" or "fragmented" authoritarian governing structure, China's local officials have long enjoyed leeway in implementing central policies in their areas of jurisdiction. Specifically in the religious policy realm, local officials have been selective in how and upon whom to implement repressive policies. How do we explain the local officials' selective implementation of religious policies? I argue that officials' selective repression varies with Party priorities and local relationships. Specifically, the center's priorities communicated to local officials determine the officials' style of repression, and combined with the officials' view of the church then determine the target of repression. The applicability of the explanation is borne out through 120 interviews with Chinese religious leaders and officials. The research reveals that the ways in which religious policies have been, and are currently being, implemented at the local level have important implications for Chinese domestic policymaking as well as the society at large.

title: Epidemiological Transition and the Crisis of the Treatment Model: The Need for a Shift Toward Preventive and Integrative Healthcare

detail.title: Epidemiological Transition and the Crisis of the Treatment Model: The Need for a Shift Toward Preventive and Integrative Healthcare

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Background: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for the majority of global mortality, yet healthcare systems remain largely oriented toward the treatment of acute conditions. This study examines the structural mismatch between contemporary disease patterns and healthcare system organization. Methods: A narrative analytical review was conducted using secondary data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study and World Health Organization (WHO) reports, supplemented by literature from PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar (2000-2026). Findings were interpreted using epidemiological transition theory, health systems analysis, and political economy frameworks. Results: The analysis identifies multiple structural drivers of treatment-oriented healthcare systems, including economic incentives favoring curative services, short-term political decision-making cycles, and the historical dominance of the biomedical model. These factors contribute to systematic underinvestment in prevention, rising healthcare expenditures, and persistent global inequalities in access to medical technologies, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. The current model is associated with increasing economic burden and projected losses in global productivity by 2030-2050. Conclusions: The findings indicate that the current healthcare model is structurally misaligned with population health needs. Improving health outcomes and system sustainability requires a reorientation toward prevention, long-term health metrics, and the evidence-based integration of complementary approaches within healthcare systems.

title: Does Emergency Contraception Access Reduce Adolescent Fertility? Evidence from Two Policy Reforms in Brazil
affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP, Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP and Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP

detail.title: Does Emergency Contraception Access Reduce Adolescent Fertility? Evidence from Two Policy Reforms in Brazil

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We study whether expanding access to emergency contraception (EC) through Brazil’s Unified Health System (SUS) reduced adolescent fertility and fetal mortality. Two sequential national policies provide variation: a 2005 mandate that distributed EC through primary care facilities, with a prescription requirement, and a 2012 decree that removed that prescription requirement. Exploiting cross-municipal variation in pre-determined SUS infrastructure, we estimate difference-in-differences models using a panel of 4,184 municipalities from 1999 to 2020 across five empirical designs. We find no robust evidence that either policy reduced adolescent birth rates differentially in municipalities with greater SUS primary care access (beta hat = 0.032, standard error = 0.062, p-value = 0.61). However, using DOFET fetal death records, we find suggestive evidence that the 2012 removal of the prescription requirement reduced fetal mortality in high-access municipalities (beta hat = -0.165, standard error = 0.093, p-value = 0.077). This pattern—null for birth rates and negative for fetal deaths—is consistent with EC substituting for unsafe clandestine abortions without changing the final number of live births. These results suggest that supply-side EC interventions may reduce the harm associated with unwanted pregnancies even when they do not reduce their incidence.

title: Swappable EV Batteries for Critical Infrastructure Resilience: A Multilevel Public-Private Partnership Approach
affiliations: , Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian University of Technology and Beijing Jiaotong University

detail.title: Swappable EV Batteries for Critical Infrastructure Resilience: A Multilevel Public-Private Partnership Approach
detail.abstract: The growing instability of power grids, driven by extreme weather and system failures, highlights the need for innovative urban energy resilience solutions. Electric vehicle (EV) battery swapping (BS) offers an opportunity to serve both routine mobility and emergency power supply. By staging batteries across stations, BS firms can provide rapid charging under normal conditions while enabling governments to requisition reserves during emergencies. This dual role positions BS as an effective backup for urban resilience, yet without policy intervention, firms may underinvest in battery reserves or lack incentives to share them with the government. To address this, we develop a Public-Private Partnership framework that captures strategic interactions among the government, a firm providing BS services, and EV users. At the policy level, the government designs subsidy schemes and requisition protocols to minimize social cost during emergencies. At the firm level, the commercial operator determines station locations and battery staging to maximize profit under subsidy incentives. At the operational level, EV users choose charging modes and specific stations, resulting in equilibrium demand that affects the market share and revenue of the BS firm. This hierarchical structure yields a multilevel problem with decision-dependent feasible regions, linking policy design, firm's profitability, and demand response within a unified analytical framework. To tackle the computational complexity, we adopt artificial neural networks (ANNs) as a surrogate of BS demand and derive an approximate bilevel program. We then propose a neural-embedded feasibility restoration algorithm, enhanced by several refinement techniques, to solve this program efficiently. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate the high approximation accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. Sensitivity analysis reveals a two-phase effect of subsidies: moderate subsidies are highly effective in eliminating power shortages, whereas higher subsidies primarily reduce response times but at substantially greater cost.

title: Pedestrian Evacuation Simulation Model Considering Self-Rescue Behavior under Asphyxiation and Stampede Conditions
affiliations: Yanshan University, Yanshan University, Yanshan University and Yanshan University

detail.title: Pedestrian Evacuation Simulation Model Considering Self-Rescue Behavior under Asphyxiation and Stampede Conditions
detail.abstract: Crowd-induced asphyxia and stampede accidents occur frequently in high-density crowd venues, posing severe threats to public safety. To explore the evolutionary mechanism of such accidents and characterize the complex interactions among pedestrians’ physiological states, behavioral decisions, and surrounding environments, this paper develops a hybrid simulation framework combining refined cellular automaton and the social force model. The model introduces a dual-indicator asphyxia judgment system to realize quantitative classification of asphyxia risk, incorporates the self-protection mechanism of cross-armed chest protection to quantify the buffering effect of self-rescue behaviors on thoracic pressure, considers the secondary injury mechanism driven by crowd overlapping after falls and clarifies how the number of overlapping layers accelerates casualty development, and calibrates the physio-mechanical parameters of pedestrians with different body types to accurately distinguish individual risks of asphyxiation and falling. Simulation results verify the robustness of the model, which can reproduce key dynamic characteristics of stampede events. The simulation outcomes are highly consistent with those of classic models and real accidents. Results show that cross-armed chest protection presents a dual effect of both protection and risk. Secondary injury is a critical factor aggravating casualties and reducing evacuation efficiency. Pedestrian body heterogeneity directly determines casualty types and overall safety levels. The research provides theoretical support and a simulation basis for formulating emergency evacuation strategies and differentiated risk prevention and control measures in high-density crowd venues.

title: The Constitution's Forgotten Term Limit on Military Power
affiliations: and Emory University School of Law

detail.title: The Constitution's Forgotten Term Limit on Military Power

publicationDetails.journalName: Emory University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Somewhere in the basement of American constitutional law sits a forgotten clause that the Framers considered indispensable, Alexander Hamilton defended at length in The Federalist Papers, and virtually every constitutional law professor has stopped teaching. Article I, Section 8, Clause 12 -- the "Armies Clause" or "Two-Year Clause" -- provides that no appropriation of money to "raise and support Armies" shall be "for a longer Term than two Years." It is, in the Framers' conception, the military's term limit: a structural guarantee that no single Congress could permanently fund a standing army, and that every House and every Senate would retain the power to influence the conduct and composition of any federal army by controlling its funding. 

That guarantee, enshrined in the Constitution's text, is now largely theoretical due to an obscure 1904 Solicitor General opinion that has proven to be a footnote to history-until now.  The Framers' fears are being realized:  troops are being deployed in American cities, Congress has not cast a vote on the Iran War authorization, and President Trump signed into law a four-year military and ICE funding package buried in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that insulates militarized immigration enforcement from congressional control.  In a forthcoming Article in the George Washington Law Review, we argue that it is time for all this to change; it is time to remember and revitalize the Two-Year Clause.  Here's why.

detail.abstract: We study the interconnection between the productivity and pricing effects of financial shocks. Combining administrative records on firm-level output prices and quantities with quasi-experimental variation in credit supply, we show that a tightening of credit conditions has a persistent, yet delayed, negative effect on firms' long-run physical productivity growth (TFPQ) but also induces firms to change their pricing policies. Commonly used revenue-based productivity measures (TFPR)-which conflate price and productivity-offer biased predictions regarding the consequences of financial shocks for firms' productivity growth, underestimating the long-run elasticity of physical productivity to credit supply by half. We also show that the pricing adjustments themselves have productivity implications. Firms use low pricing as a source of internal financing, allowing them to avoid cutting expenditures on productivityenhancing activities, thereby softening the impact of financial shocks. We incorporate these forces into a quantitative model of firm dynamics to quantify the importance of productivity and pricing dynamics (and their interplay) in driving the scarring effects of financial crises on aggregate productivity and welfare.
