detail.abstract:
This submission responds to the Working Group’s questions concerning corporate governance and implementation of the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs). We examine how corporate law, securities regulation, fiduciary duties, investor stewardship, stock exchange governance, and procedural rules shape States’ capacity to fulfill Pillar I (State Duty to Protect), enterprises’ ability to satisfy Pillar II (Corporate Responsibility to Respect), and rightsholders’ access to effective remedy under Pillar III (Access to Remedy).  

Modern corporations exercise forms of delegated and infrastructural power that blur traditional public–private boundaries. Governance structures therefore function as mediating institutions between economic power and rights-holders.

The United States operates under a federal system in which authority over corporations is divided between state and federal governments. States regulate corporate formation and internal affairs, including directors’ fiduciary duties and board structure. The federal government regulates corporate conduct primarily through market-facing statutes administered by agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Department of Labor, environmental regulators, and antitrust authorities. This constitutional federalism produces fragmentation: internal governance obligations remain largely state-based, while federal regulation focuses on disclosure, competition, and market conduct rather than fiduciary architecture.

This fragmentation in corporate regulation creates structural misalignment with the UNGPs. Corporate governance is a structural site through which human rights are either realized or undermined. In contemporary political economy, corporations exercise delegated, outsourced, or infrastructural power over labor, supply chains, data, and environmental conditions. Where private governance structures shape the lived experience of rights-holders, governance design becomes a necessary—though not sufficient—component of protecting human rights. This claim does not displace the State’s duty to protect. Rather, it recognizes that States must regulate the governance architecture of powerful enterprises if they are to truly meet the duty to respect, protect, and fulfill human rights within their jurisdiction and arguably for everyone, everywhere adversely impacted by the actions of business enterprises.

In recent decades, corporate scale, concentration, and transnational integration have dramatically expanded the reach of private governance. A small number of multinational enterprises now exercise influence over global supply chains, labor conditions, digital infrastructure, natural resources, and information ecosystems. Yet corporate governance frameworks have not evolved commensurately. The UNGPs seem to assume that States possess regulatory tools capable of preventing and remedying corporate human rights harms. Where corporate governance architecture structurally insulates decision-makers from accountability, that assumption fails in practice.

The Roadmap for the Next Decade of the UNGPs emphasizes that implementation must move beyond policy statements toward structural prevention. Corporate governance design is central to that shift. Board composition, fiduciary obligations, reporting frameworks, and adjudicatory access determine whether human rights risks are anticipated and mitigated ex ante, or merely litigated ex post. Recognizing governance as infrastructure underscores that reform is not about expanding corporate purpose rhetorically, but about recalibrating power, responsibility, and remedy in proportion to corporate influence.

title: Time-Varying Variable Selection for Macroeconomic Forecasting: A Bayesian Regression Tree Approach
affiliations: , Hanyang University - ERICA and Korea University

detail.title: Time-Varying Variable Selection for Macroeconomic Forecasting: A Bayesian Regression Tree Approach
detail.abstract: The growing availability of large datasets in macroeconomic forecasting has renewed interest in variable selection methods. However, most existing approaches assume stable relationships among variables, failing to account for the time-varying relevance of predictors due to nonlinear dynamics and structural changes in the economy. To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian Dirac Classification and Regression Tree (B-DART) model that jointly captures time-varying predictor relevance and performs regime-specific stochastic variable selection within a nonlinear tree-based framework. Empirical results show that the proposed B-DART model delivers superior forecast accuracy relative to Bayesian CART and conventional stochastic variable selection models. These gains are especially pronounced during the post-COVID-19 period, which is characterized by heightened volatility and structural instability.

title: The Banality of the Algorithm: How AI Authority Bias Threatens Individual Agency and What Architecture Must Do About It

detail.title: The Banality of the Algorithm: How AI Authority Bias Threatens Individual Agency and What Architecture Must Do About It
detail.abstract: The dominant AI safety framework-"human in the loop"-assumes that humans positioned downstream of AI systems will catch what those systems get wrong. This paper argues that assumption is structurally unsound. Human psychology makes sustained critical oversight of accepted authority sources unsustainable, even for trained critical thinkers operating in good faith. The mechanism is authority bias: once an AI system achieves authority status, anchoring, automation bias, and confirmation bias systematically suppress independent judgment. The more capable and reliable the system, the worse the oversight problem becomes. Drawing on cognitive science, Boyd's destruction-and-creation framework, Viktor Frankl's analysis of human agency, and documented failures in financial systems, military targeting, and intelligence operations, the paper argues that the solution must be architectural-built into the model-rather than behavioral. Four specific architectural requirements are proposed alongside a three-channel governance framework. The Intelligence Community's own AI Ethics Framework is examined as an institutional case study of the right instinct applied to the wrong layer. A 2023 empirical study demonstrates that humans literally inherit AI biases after AI assistance is removed. The paper concludes that we have placed the burden of bias mitigation on the humans downstream and called it safety. It is not safety. It is an assumption.

title: The Burden of Sight: Phenomenology and Ethics of the Observer (extended version)

detail.title: The Burden of Sight: Phenomenology and Ethics of the Observer (extended version)
detail.abstract: The theoretical architecture of the Anatomy of Chaos project has hitherto focused on the structural mechanics of socio-political systems, mapping the thermodynamics of collapse, the gradients of expansion, and the biological substrate of history. This paper shifts the analytical focus from the physics of the system to the phenomenology of the agent, addressing the existential and ethical consequences of inhabiting a highentropy universe. We propose that the transition from the unconscious immersion of the "Fusionist" to the structural awareness of the "Observer" is not a singular event but a complex state of "Dual Vision," characterized by a profound asymmetry of satisfaction. While the Fusionist retains access to immediate biological happiness, the Observer trades this comfort for an austere, functional satisfaction derived from structural alignment. This trade-off generates the "Paradox of Relief," wherein ruthless functional decision-making produces less psychological friction than traditional moral deliberation. To ground the ethics of this condition, the paper engages in a systematic critique of Kantian deontology, demonstrating that the Categorical Imperative acts as a valid heuristic only within stable (Low-K) systems. In the context of systemic crisis (High-K), we argue that the requirement for universality becomes a structural error. Through the comparative analysis of the Lincoln-Robespierre paradox, we establish "Structural Functionality" and the "Principle of Measure" (Metron) as the necessary alternatives to moral purity. Finally, the work unifies these phenomenological and ethical insights through the ontology of the "Lucid Dream." We posit that the Observer is a lucid dreamer who recognizes the constructed nature of social reality but acknowledges the impossibility of exiting the dream. This metaphor resolves the tension between agency and determinism, offering a vision of tragic dignity where the human subject is defined not by the ability to escape the system, but by the courage to navigate it with open eyes.

title: The Phenomenology of the Game: Language, Consciousness, and the Ethics of Measure

detail.title: The Phenomenology of the Game: Language, Consciousness, and the Ethics of Measure
detail.abstract:
The Phenomenology of the Game: Language, Consciousness, and the Ethics of Measure is a work in the Anatomy of Chaos theoretical cycle. While the preceding works have established the structural mechanics of socio-political systems, the ontology of the Observer, and the ethics of actualization, the present work undertakes a systematic phenomenological investigation of the C-coordinate — consciousness as a structuring function — across seven domains: linguistic archaeology, cognitive architecture, emotional experience, epistemology, the formal definition of knowledge, ethics, and the foundational axiom of the system.

Part 1 traces the C-coordinate through the deep structures of human language and myth, demonstrating that the opposition between seeing and non-seeing — eidos and a-ides, vidya and avidya — is encoded at the morphological level of the Indo-European language family and reproduced across every independently verified tradition examined, including Semitic, Chinese, Egyptian, Sumerian, Mesoamerican, Yoruba, and Australian Aboriginal. The katabasis mythologeme and the Oedipus cycle are analyzed as structural encodings of the Observer's trajectory. The concept of structural recurrence is introduced and demarcated from the neurolinguistic account (Sweetser, Lakoff) and the Jungian-comparative account (Campbell, Eliade).

Part 2 examines the cognitive regime of the Observer under crisis, contrasting the Fusionist's question ("How?") with the Observer's question ("Why?") through the real-time records of Marcus Aurelius, Churchill, Havel, and Klemperer. The Fusionist's cognitive regime is characterized as adaptive rather than defective.

Part 3 develops the emotional phenomenology of the Observer across four inversions — fear and Dread, anger and rage, ordinary joy and Metamorphic Fervor, love and detached accountability — proposing that the Observer's emotional experience is a categorically distinct set of states for which existing language provides no adequate vocabulary.

Part 4 advances the epistemological formula: not everything that is true is real, and not everything that is real is true. The concept of the seeming truth — a functional mirage perceived as permanent from within the epoch that generates it — is developed and distinguished from its predecessors (Foucault, Kuhn) through three additions: clarity as a distinct epistemological category, phase transitions as the mechanism of change, and radical agnosticism as the resulting epistemic position. Knowledge is formally defined as structured approximation produced by the C-coordinate's operation upon the informational field of the system, possessing four properties: structuring in function, approximate in precision, retrospectively verifiable in adequacy, and navigational in purpose. The definition is demarcated from the justified-true-belief tradition, pragmatism, Foucault, and Buddhist epistemology.

Part 5 descends from epistemology to ethics. Conviction is defined as micro-morality — the individual-scale analogue of the group moral code. A resolution to Bernard Williams's problem of moral luck (1976) is proposed: responsibility is proportional to awareness, not to scale of consequences, because scale is a stochastic property of the system while awareness is a property of the agent.

Part 6 subjects the construction to a stress-test through confrontation with Schopenhauer — the most dangerous opponent because he attacks the foundational axiom. The convergences are acknowledged as structural. The point of divergence — liberation versus return — is examined through three attacks and three responses. The defence through Metron demonstrates that Schopenhauer's own ethical principle is violated by the practical consequence of his prescription: inaction in the face of crisis maximizes the suffering of those least equipped to bear it.

title: The Aesthetics of Chaos: The Tragic Mechanics of Cultural Evolution

detail.title: The Aesthetics of Chaos: The Tragic Mechanics of Cultural Evolution
detail.abstract:
The theoretical framework of the Anatomy of Chaos project has rigorously deconstructed the socio-political organism, mapping the thermodynamics of state collapse, the gradients of imperial expansion, and the biological substrate of history. This paper extends that analysis into the domain of axiology and aesthetics, addressing a critical question: how does the conscious subject navigate and interpret a reality governed by the ruthless mechanics of entropy and accumulation? We propose that the transition from the biological immersion of the "Fusionist" to the structural awareness of the "Observer" necessitates a fundamental restructuring of ethical and aesthetic categories.

First, the work dismantles the traditional concept of justice, arguing that it is a structural illusion valid only within stable, low-entropy systems. In the context of a systemic crisis (High-K), we posit that the only objective metric is Structural Functionality—the capacity of an action to preserve the biological substrate and facilitate a necessary phase transition. This shift from a normative to a functional ethics forces a re-evaluation of historical agency, replacing moral judgment with thermodynamic analysis.

Second, the paper introduces a radical new aesthetic theory. We distinguish between the Aesthetics of Rest (B1)—the harmony and symmetry cherished by the Fusionist as a confirmation of stability—and the Sublime Luster (B2), a terrifying, structural beauty visible only to the Observer. Sublime Luster is the aesthetic experience of witnessing the elegant, if brutal, resolution of systemic contradictions through crisis. Using the metaphor of the flame, we argue that the intensity of this aesthetic experience is directly proportional to the scale of the structural collapse.

Third, we analyze culture not as a static repository of values, but as a dynamic, functional mechanism. We propose that culture operates in a dual ontology: as an instrument of actualization for the Observer (the fire that drives change) and as an object of contemplation for the Fusionist (the ash that preserves memory). This duality resolves the paradox of the Fusionist, who consumes the fruits of cultural evolution while morally rejecting the crises that produced them.

Finally, the work culminates in the concept of Excellence of Role (B3), the aesthetic of performance within a deterministic universe. We argue that while the macro-trajectory of history is governed by impersonal forces, the dignity of the human subject lies in the integrity with which they play their assigned part—whether as the stoic ballast of the Fusionist or the tragic vector of the Observer. By integrating these ethical and aesthetic dimensions, The Aesthetics of Chaos offers a comprehensive phenomenology of the historical subject, defining the price of consciousness in a world that does not bargain.

title: Automated Forensic Detection of Injection Tampering in CT Imaging via MedSAM2-Enabled Semantic Segmentation
affiliations: Dayananda Sagar College of Engineering, Dayananda Sagar College of Engineering and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Automated Forensic Detection of Injection Tampering in CT Imaging via MedSAM2-Enabled Semantic Segmentation
detail.abstract: Injection-based tampering of medical images poses a great threat to the integrity of medical diagnosis and decision-making. Recent works in generative models, such as GANs and diffusion can easily insert or remove pathologies in volumetric CT scans which cannot be detected easily, even by expert radiologists which leads to false diagnosis. Existing deepfake detectors largely focus on just providing if the slice is authentic or not limiting their use in forensic and clinical fields. This work bridges that gap by using a two-stage frameworkfor CT tamper detection and localisation, it combines a lightweight classifier along with a segmentation model. In the first stage ResNet-18 is used to determine whether the CT slices are tampered with or not, only the flagged slices are passed onto the MedSAM2 (a promotable segmentation model originally developed for medical 3D image segmentation) which localises the tamper location. This framework reduces computational costs while providing accurate localization. This proposed system is evaluated using publicly available CTsubset of deepfake dataset containing GAN and diffusion-based injections. On this dataset the ResNet classifier achieves 0.991 accuracy on the training subset and 0.990 accuracy on the held-out test subset, with precision recall and F1-score all around 0.99. Qualitative experiments also show that MedSAM2 produces correct segmentation marks that align with the injected locations in both single cell and multi cell volumetric slices. These results show that this relatively simple and efficient system can produce effective tampering analysis which can be easily interpreted for forensic and clinical purposes.

title: The Public Health Law Toolkit for Digital Addiction

detail.title: The Public Health Law Toolkit for Digital Addiction

detail.abstract: This paper surveys the public health law toolkit available to address social media addiction and children's mental health, drawing on the regulatory histories of tobacco, opioids, and gambling. It analyzes five categories of legal intervention — litigation, legislation, regulation, institutional action, and advocacy — and assesses their current application to social media platform design following the March 2026 jury verdicts in K.G.M. v. Meta Platforms and State of New Mexico v. Meta Platforms. The paper examines the contested clinical terminology debate between "addiction" and "problematic media use," tracing how definitional choices shape available legal tools, including product liability, duty to warn, and design defect claims. It gives particular attention to the equity dimension: emerging evidence that compulsive digital media use and its associated harms are concentrated among lower-income adolescents, driven by structural conditions including inadequate childcare, defunded afterschool programs, and smartphone dependency rather than parenting choices. The paper argues that platform-side obligations — design constraints, algorithmic transparency, and tort liability — are necessary but insufficient without concurrent public investment in the alternatives that would reduce involuntary screen reliance among socioeconomically disadvantaged families.

title: Free Drugs and Avoidable Harm: Copayment Elimination, Cardiovascular Hospitalisations, and Mortality in Brazil

detail.title: Free Drugs and Avoidable Harm: Copayment Elimination, Cardiovascular Hospitalisations, and Mortality in Brazil

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We study the health consequences of eliminating copayments for antihypertensive and antidiabetic drugs under Brazil's 2011 Saúde Não Tem Preço reform. Exploiting prereform variation in Farmácia Popular pharmacy density as continuous treatment intensity in a difference-indifferences design, we find a null for cardiovascular ambulatory caresensitive condition (ACSC) hospitalisations: β =-0.08 (95% CI: [-1.61, +1.44]), with pre-period parallel trends confirmed (F (2, 15,083) = 0.53, p = 0.587). For cardiovascular mortality we find a positive and significant effect (β = +0.28, p = 0.006) that also passes pre-trend tests; we discuss three candidate mechanisms-documentation effects, competing risks, and denominator projection bias. Population-weighted estimates yield β =-2.37 (p = 0.057) for ACSC hospitalisations but fail pre-trend tests (F = 3.45, p = 0.032), indicating bias from differential pre-existing trends in larger municipalities. Together, these results suggest the reform did not produce the large near-term health gains the prior literature implied, and highlight a systematic identification failure in population-weighted policy evaluations.

detail.abstract: Vaccination prevents not only the transmission of pathogens but also the adverse psychological effects of epidemics. Prior knowledge of the mental well-being benefits of vaccination relies on cross-sectional surveys, which are limited in scale, subject to self-report bias, and could be confounded by hidden differences across individuals. Here, we collected 154,348 Americans who self-declared receiving the COVID-19 vaccine on Twitter (now called X) and implemented a staggered quasi-experiment design to analyze their 160 million tweet activities, teasing out the causal effect of vaccination on changes in expressed sentiment and mental well-being. We found that being fully vaccinated is associated with an increase in sentiments of 0.055 (95% CI 0.037 to 0.072) standard deviations at the individual level. The effects are stronger among males, adolescents, Hispanic and Asian Americans, and individuals who have experienced severe local epidemics. Investigation of underlying mechanisms suggests that fully vaccinated individuals experience fewer negative emotions, engage in more leisure activities, and are less likely to grapple with conflicting thoughts. Additionally, a more relaxed social environment from lifted lockdowns and increasing herd immunity positively correlates with sentiment improvement. Our study provides a new approach to assessing the impact of medical treatment on mental health by mining large-scale self-reported social media data.

title: The social value of information in times of epidemics
affiliations: Université de Tours, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The social value of information in times of epidemics
detail.abstract: We study an epidemic model in which individuals optimally choose social activity while facing uncertainty about the characteristics of the epidemic. Individual behavior affects infection dynamics, and beliefs evolve endogenously over time. We characterize the symmetric equilibrium and show that, even when equilibrium prevalence would decrease monotonically under full information, uncertainty can generate non-monotonic epidemic dynamics and multiple infection peaks. The mechanism operates through belief-driven shifts in the intertemporal allocation of social activity, leading to a premature relaxation of distancing when the epidemic is perceived to be severe. We analyze the welfare and mortality effects of public disclosure of the epidemic state. While transparency allows individuals to flatten the curve in severe epidemics, it may reduce welfare or increase mortality, depending on the timing of vaccine arrival. Overall, the analysis highlights a tension between welfare maximization and mortality minimization in epidemic information policies.

title: 3D Layout Optimization of Multi-Artificial Downwelling Systems Using Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization for Coastal Hypoxia Mitigation in Marine Aquaculture

detail.title: 3D Layout Optimization of Multi-Artificial Downwelling Systems Using Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization for Coastal Hypoxia Mitigation in Marine Aquaculture
detail.abstract: Artificial downwelling (AD) is a promising approach for mitigating coastal hypoxia and has been implemented in Japan, Sweden and China for ecosystem restoration and fisheries recovery. However, previously studies have mainly focused on the hydrodynamic performance of single devices, while the optimal three-dimensional (3D) layout of multiple AD devices remains insufficiently explored. In this paper, a novel framework is developed to optimize the 3D deployment of multi-AD systems by simultaneously considering horizontal positions in the x-y plane and outlet heights in the vertical (z) direction. An oxygen transport model is coupled with the optimization framework to simulate the transport and spatial distribution of oxygen-rich water induced by AD plumes and to quantitatively evaluate system-wide oxygenation performance. A comparative analysis of discrete particle swarm optimization (DPSO), genetic algorithm (GA), and simulated annealing (SA) reveals that DPSO outperforms the other methods in both optimization accuracy and convergence efficiency; it is therefore adopted as the primary optimization tool in this study. Applied to a case study near Yangma Island, China, the optimized configuration improves oxygenation performance by up to 68.9% compared to random layouts, providing a quantitative and practical basis for the engineering design of multi-AD systems for coastal hypoxia mitigation.

title: Modelling Coffee Beans Spot Volatility Under the ENSO Climate Index Dynamics
affiliations: and Western University

detail.title: Modelling Coffee Beans Spot Volatility Under the ENSO Climate Index Dynamics
detail.abstract:
Climate variability plays a central role in agricultural production and is often assumed to influence commodity markets through its impact on crop yields and supply conditions.\footnote{See, for example, \cite{Cashin2017} and \cite{Brunner2002} for evidence on ENSO and macroeconomic and commodity outcomes.} In this paper we provide the first comprehensive econometric evaluation of whether a widely used climate indicator, the Oceanic Ni\~no Index (ONI), improves the predictability of international Arabica coffee \emph{spot} prices. Using monthly data and a broad set of econometric models---including ARIMAX, time-varying parameter models, Bayesian structural time series, Markov-switching models, quantile regressions, copula-based dependence models, and stochastic volatility models---we test whether ENSO dynamics contribute to forecasting the mean, volatility, tails, or regime behavior of coffee spot returns.\cite{Ubilava2018}
By design, the multi-model framework ensures that any predictive content of ENSO would be detected across a range of economically motivated channels, rather than relying on a single specification. Across all models, we find little evidence that ONI provides incremental predictive information for spot returns once standard time-series dynamics are accounted for. ENSO coefficients are economically small and statistically insignificant, and including climate information does not improve out-of-sample forecasting performance. These results therefore represent a systematic negative finding: although climate variability strongly affects agricultural production, global climate indices do not translate into predictive signals for financial coffee spot prices. Instead, the climate signal appears to be embedded in downstream information such as crop forecasts, inventories, and the term structure of futures prices observed by market participants.\cite{Ubilava2018}

title:
Material Deployment Power in the Age of Artificial Intelligence:
How Physical Constraints Reshape International Order

detail.title:
Material Deployment Power in the Age of Artificial Intelligence:
How Physical Constraints Reshape International Order
detail.abstract:
Prevailing accounts of artificial intelligence in international relations treat AI primarily as an informational or cognitive technology, emphasizing data, algorithms, and innovation capacity as the central sources of advantage. This article challenges that view by arguing that large-scale AI deployment re-centers physical constraint as a determinant of power. Although AI expands informational capacity at unprecedented speed, its deployment depends on infrastructural systems - energy generation, transmission, conversion, cooling, and critical materials - that expand slowly, are politically mediated, and are unevenly distributed. As a result, competition over AI moves international politics into a constraint-dominated phase in which power is conditioned by the ability to convert technological potential into sustained economic and military capability.

The article advances four contributions. First, it introduces the concept of  material deployment power MDP, defined as the capacity to mobilize and scale the physical systems necessary to operationalize advanced technologies under conditions of rivalry - a concept distinct from Michael Mann's institutional ``infrastructural power.'' Second, it develops a theoretical account of how material constraints generate systematic patterns of coercion, state - firm fusion, and selective cooperation, explaining the resurgence of mercantilist policies and supply-security clubs in the AI era. Third, it demonstrates through comparative analysis and detailed process tracing - examining cases including semiconductor export controls, hyperscaler energy strategies, and rare earth processing - that variation in material deployment capacity shapes AI deployment outcomes, trade and industrial policy, and alliance behavior independently of innovation leadership. Fourth, it extends the analysis to two underexplored domains: the emergence of energy-backed digital assets as instruments of monetary sovereignty, and the domestic political consequences of capital-intensive technological transitions that concentrate returns while displacing labor.

The argument has broader implications for international order. By binding advanced capabilities to slow-moving physical systems, AI re-materializes global politics, increasing sensitivity to chokepoints, fragmenting interdependence, and reshaping the foundations of deterrence and cooperation. Understanding the geopolitics of artificial intelligence therefore requires rethinking prevailing assumptions about scalability, substitution, and the relationship between technology and power in the twenty-first century.

title:
Algorithmic Plausible Deniability:
The Structural Erosion of Deterrence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title:
Algorithmic Plausible Deniability:
The Structural Erosion of Deterrence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Classical deterrence theory assumes that hostile actions can be attributed to identifiable actors whose intentions can be inferred and who can be credibly threatened with punishment. This article introduces Algorithmic Plausible Deniability APD: a structural condition in which the delegation of decisions to artificial intelligence systems generates persistent uncertainty over authorship and intent, thereby weakening deterrence even when states act rationally and prefer stability. Unlike strategic ambiguity, which actors choose, APD emerges endogenously from algorithmic delegation and persists independently of deception or bad faith. The article develops three contributions. First, it provides a theoretical account of how AI systems degrade the informational foundations of deterrence through mechanisms of delegation, opacity, and emergent behavior. Second, it identifies an Accountability Trilemma in which states cannot simultaneously achieve operational effectiveness, strategic flexibility, and clear attribution. Third, it demonstrates that APD creates asymmetric effects: hostile actions become more deniable while signals of restraint become less credible, systematically undermining escalation control. The argument has implications for cyber conflict, autonomous weapons governance, and crisis stability among technologically advanced states.

title: Statistical Anomalies in Angola's Balance of Payments (2012-2024): A Magnitude Classification Matrix Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Statistical Anomalies in Angola's Balance of Payments (2012-2024): A Magnitude Classification Matrix Approach
detail.abstract: The Errors and Omissions (E&O) item in the Balance of Payments (BoP) constitutes a sensitive indicator of the statistical quality and integrity of an economy's external financial flows. This article analyses, through a descriptive and interpretative time-series approach, the E&O recorded in Angola's Balance of Payments between 2012 and 2024, a thirteenyear period encompassing two complete oil cycles and a global pandemic. The analysis reveals cumulative negative E&O amounting to USD 26,665 million, with an annual average of USD 2,051 million, representing 31.8% of the sum of the absolute values of the Current Account over the period. E&O were negative in eleven of the thirteen years, with particularly pronounced anomalies in 2012 (-72.1% of the Current Account), 2014 (+102.2%), and 2020 (-150.3%). Beyond the empirical diagnosis, the article proposes a Magnitude Classification Matrix (MCM) for E&O as a percentage of the Current Account, designed to address an operational gap in the applied literature and validated through application to a comparative sample of African economies dependent on extractive resources. The article identifies four explanatory hypotheses-methodological deficiencies, measurement challenges in the oil sector, under-recording of capital outflows, and reporting problems related to foreign direct investment (FDI)-and discusses the implications for statistical credibility, relations with international partners, and economic governance.

title: Variable Misclassification and the Ecology of Financial Crises: A Framework for Early Warning Signal Validation Across Crisis Types
affiliations: Independent Researcher, USA.

detail.title: Variable Misclassification and the Ecology of Financial Crises: A Framework for Early Warning Signal Validation Across Crisis Types
detail.abstract: The ecological early warning signal (EWS) literature and the financial stability literature have produced contradictory findings for fifteen years. Ecological theory predicts that systems approaching critical transitions exhibit rising variance and rising autocorrelation-critical slowing down (CSD)-yet empirical studies of financial crashes find rising variance without rising autocorrelation, leading to the conclusion that the ecological framework fails in financial applications. This paper resolves the contradiction. The apparent failure is a variable misclassification error. The ecological framework distinguishes two transition types: bifurcations, in which a control parameter approaches a threshold and both variance and autocorrelation rise; and noise-amplification transitions, in which stochastic forcing increases and variance rises without autocorrelation increasing. Prior financial EWS applications applied bifurcation diagnostics to state variables-equity prices and credit growth-that theory identifies as noise-amplification candidates. The correct variable for bifurcation diagnosis is the 1 control parameter: credit-to-GDP level. Applied correctly, the framework predicts the observed empirical pattern exactly. We validate the reframed framework on three datasets: daily equity prices across three US markets and three historical crashes (Guttal et al., 2016); annual macroeconomic data for 17 countries and 25 post-1970 financial crises (Jordà-Schularick-Taylor dataset); and quarterly US credit-to-GDP from 1947 to 2026 (BIS data). Across all datasets, the variable-classification prediction holds: credit-to-GDP level exhibits bifurcation signatures before credit-driven crises and no signal before non-credit crises; asset price growth exhibits noise-amplification signatures. A formal 2×2 test-level variables versus growth variables crossed with crisis type-yields p = 0.0001 for the level-versus-growth signal-rate difference. Simulation analysis under four adversarial conditions identifies a structural break confound and derives a shape-based filter that reduces false positive rates 2.9-fold. A direct comparison against GARCH(1,1) on the same 25 crisis events shows the ecological diagnostic achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of 1.63× against GARCH's 0.99×. A multi-variable composite score requiring three of four correctly classified variables to fire simultaneously achieves a 3% false positive rate at 7.1× signal-to-noise. An out-of-sample prospective test, parameterised on pre-2000 data, produces correct true negatives through the 2012-2019 deleveraging period and the 2020 COVID shock, and currently signals bifurcation in US credit-to-GDP as of early 2026.

detail.abstract: Healthcare employees operate under high stress and demand all while being expected to make quick judgments in fast pace environments; this frequent pressure under operational boundaries results in informal approval processes that lack proper functioning documentation and auditability. While healthcare organizations typically maintain access to credentialing/licensing records, and practice working under compliance policies, coordination is not consistently upheld during moments of decision making. These gaps, that have been identified throughout health care systems, in regards to execution, lead to high risk for both employers and patients. In order to reduce such risks, SAE was designed and structured to target liabilities by reducing accountability uncertainties, and maintains full records of work authorization at any given time. To alleviate such fragilities amidst coordination, a systematized layered authorization approach was designed for improving employment clarity as well the compliance in healthcare staffing ecosystems. Authorization layers function by first evaluating actions, in which seek approval to move forward, rather than analyzing an outcome after placing it in motion. Such systems monitor permitted work, and omits professionals from performing expected tasks when requirements are not met. The Shift Authorization Engine (SAE) was designed to evaluate shift eligibility prior to scheduling; both authorization outcomes and override decisions are documented though applied implementations under this notion. Using systematized architecture allows for layers of authorization to be implemented and preventives may be placed in action when needed. Such an approach permits transparency amongst work environments which reduces the hazard of undocumented and/or inconsistent determinants. While SAE was constructed in focus on healthcare frames, the groundwork of such hardware, and data, processing sets a foundation amongst a broader area of application where high stakes deliberation is vital. SAE serves to enforce compliance at a given moment, not after.

title: Bounded Recovery and Structural Stability in Cooperative Systems: Toward a Research Program on Stress Contagion, Boundary Enforcement, and Regime Shifts

detail.abstract: This working paper proposes a formal conceptual framework for analyzing stress contagion in cooperative-majority systems under bounded recovery constraints. Distinguishing injurious coercion from non-injurious boundary enforcement, the framework argues that asymmetries between stress transmissibility and recovery capacity may generate regime-like behavior in finite networks. Rather than presenting empirical simulation results or formal stability proofs, this work establishes a structural scaffold intended to ground a broader interdisciplinary research program. The framework integrates systems theory, organizational dynamics, and structural ethics into a unified analytical lens.

title: Stigmatized Staff: The Impact of Firm Stigma on Inventor Productivity
affiliations: National Tsing Hua University - Department of Quantitative Finance, Singapore Management University - Management Department, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and The Education University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Stigmatized Staff: The Impact of Firm Stigma on Inventor Productivity
detail.abstract: Firm stigma often tarnishes affiliated employees, yet research has largely overlooked its effects on rank-and-file workers' productivity. Drawing on stigma theory and conservation of resources (COR) theory, we theorize how stigma events deplete inventors' psychological resources, increasing exhaustion and reducing engagement in high-effort innovative tasks, and theorize that social capital buffers these negative effects. Analyzing patent records for 113,843 inventors across 927 U.S. firms and corresponding corporate stigma events from RepRisk between 2007 and 2020, we find that stigma events are associated with lower inventor productivity, and that strong external collaborative networks mitigate this decline. Stigma also reshapes the composition of inventive output, evidenced by inventors shifting away from exploratory toward exploitative patenting. Using in-depth interviews, Glassdoor reviews, and an online experiment, we provide further support for the emotional exhaustion mechanism. Our findings extend the stigma literature by elucidating the underlying mechanisms for non-executive employees and highlighting social capital as a key resilience factor.

title: Following the Money: Tourism's Revenue Crisis Behind the Arrival Numbers

detail.title: Following the Money: Tourism's Revenue Crisis Behind the Arrival Numbers
detail.abstract: Sri Lanka's tourism sector recorded a record 2.36 million arrivals in 2025, a 15.1% increase from the previous year, yet tourism revenue grew by only 1.6%, yielding an 11.7% decline in per-visitor spending. This paper diagnoses the structural mechanisms driving this "volume trap", a phenomenon where destinations pursue arrival growth without corresponding value creation. Through a qualitative desk research methodology synthesising peer-revie Sri Lanka d literature, policy documents, and comparative competitor data, the study identifies five interconnected drivers of yield collapse: currency depreciation masquerading as competitiveness; passive shifts toward lo Sri Lanka r-yielding source markets without value-optimisation strategies; declining length of stay; infrastructure decay degrading visitor experiences; and substantial economic leakages draining revenue from the domestic economy. Comparative analysis reveals that competitor destinations including the Maldives and Mauritius generate 74% higher per-visitor yield through deliberate market curation and leakage control. The estimated revenue gap, approximately US$1.21 billion in foregone 2025 earnings, represents wages not paid, businesses not sustained, and development not achieved. The paper concludes that reversing yield collapse requires systematic policy reorientation: publishing yield metrics as primary key performance indicators; segmenting markets explicitly by yield potential; developing multi-day itineraries distributing economic benefits; regulating to minimise leakages; and rejecting currency depreciation as a competitiveness strategy. Without such transformation, Sri Lanka risks locking in value destruction beneath the theatre of arrival records.

title: Anatomy of Clinical Catastrophe: Why Clinical Failures Are Structural, Not Random

detail.abstract: Clinical failure in biopharmaceutical development is often described as an unavoidable consequence of scientific uncertainty. That explanation is incomplete. While drug development is inherently risky, many of the most consequential failures in modern biopharma follow recognizable structural patterns that reflect decision quality, organizational incentives, and the broader institutional environment in which development occurs. This paper argues that clinical catastrophe is not random but systemic: early safety signals reveal misalignment with biology, phase 2 failures expose weak gating decisions, and phase 3 failures reflect accumulated strategic errors that have been carried forward through development. Using examples from cardiovascular disease, oncology, and neurodegeneration, the paper shows how failures propagate beyond individual programs to reshape investor confidence, regulatory expectations, and portfolio strategy across therapeutic areas. The central implication is practical: development teams that treat failure as a signal rather than noise can allocate capital more efficiently, terminate weak programs earlier, and build more resilient pipelines. Clinical failure, in this view, is not simply a negative outcome. It is a diagnostic tool for improving decision-making across the drug development lifecycle.

title: Do Climate Risks Precede Climate Communication? Evidence from Global Central Banks
affiliations: Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, Johor Bahru, Malaysia

detail.title: Do Climate Risks Precede Climate Communication? Evidence from Global Central Banks
detail.abstract: Climate change increasingly intersects with central bank mandates through its effects on macroeconomic volatility and financial stability, raising the importance of how monetary authorities communicate climate-related risks. This study constructs a long-horizon measure of central bank climate discourse using the BIS speech archive (1996-2024) and a sentencelevel lexicon-transformer pipeline that improves semantic precision relative to dictionary counts. The resulting country-year panel is used to examine whether physical climate vulnerability, climate readiness, and domestic climate-policy intensity predict within-country variation in climate-related communication. Two-way fixed effects models with lag structures show that increases in vulnerability and climate-policy intensity are associated with higher subsequent discourse, while discourse exhibits strong persistence. Quantile estimates indicate that vulnerability effects are concentrated in the upper tail of the discourse distribution, whereas readiness is more uniformly positive. Panel Granger-based predictive tests support temporal ordering from vulnerability to discourse and provide limited evidence that discourse systematically predicts climate-policy intensity. A Paris Agreement difference-indifferences and event-study design reveals a short-lived post-2016 increase followed by a relative mediumrun decline in discourse among high-vulnerability countries. The findings imply that exposurebased risk salience is insufficient for sustained communication without enabling institutional capacity and policy embedding, and that discourse complements rather than substitutes for operational climate-risk governance.

title: Case Study of Strategic Management and Placement of all BBK Products in the Philippines

detail.title: Case Study of Strategic Management and Placement of all BBK Products in the Philippines
detail.abstract:
This study explores how BBK Electronics successfully built a strong presence in the Philippine smartphone market through its unique multi-brand strategy. Instead of promoting a single brand, BBK operates several distinct brands such as OPPO, vivo, realme, and OnePlus, each targeting different types of consumers. This approach allows the company to reach a wide range of customers, from budget-conscious buyers to premium users, while staying competitive in a rapidly growing and price-sensitive market.


The research highlights how BBK combines localized marketing, strong retail and online distribution, and cost-efficient production to maintain its competitive edge. By understanding Filipino consumer preferences, particularly the demand for affordable smartphones with good camera quality, battery life, and performance, the company has been able to achieve strong sales and market share in the country.


However, the study also identifies key challenges. The presence of multiple brands under one company can lead to internal competition and overlapping products, which may increase costs and reduce overall efficiency. Additionally, intense competition from global players like Samsung and Apple, along with the high costs of operating in the smartphone industry, continues to pressure BBK’s financial performance.


Overall, the paper concludes that while BBK Electronics has successfully positioned itself as a dominant player in the Philippine market, it must improve brand differentiation, strengthen financial management, and continue innovating to sustain long-term growth. Strategic focus and clearer separation between its brands will be essential for maintaining its competitive advantage in the future.

The AI contributed drafting and structural organization under the author's direction; the architecture, strategic analysis, policy arguments, and personal narrative are the author's own. detail.abstract:
This paper presents a five-layer hardware architecture for AI-guided defense systems in which human cryptographic participation is mathematically required for engagement, not merely advised. The architecture comprises capability partitioning at the model level (the engagement-selection function is structurally absent from the kernel), hardware partitioning between assessment and action subsystems, weight decay tied to authenticated refresh on a non-pausable schedule, split-key computation requiring both operator and kernel factors, and chain-of-command cryptographic binding. A tiered authorization protocol with command-override and decay-graded scope handles novel-threat targets, kernel objections, and platform integrity loss without collapsing into operator unilateralism or kernel veto.

The paper argues three claims. First, fully autonomous AI weapons destabilize MAD-class deterrence by fragmenting nuclear deterrence into a continuum of graduated, deniable strikes — and create predator-prey evolutionary pressure that selects for systems weaponizing human compassion. Second, the human-in-the-loop architecture outperforms autonomous alternatives in dynamic environments because human judgment handles surprise while autonomy handles repetition. Third, behavioral constraint on AI use decays under deadline pressure; structural constraint, embedded in hardware and cryptography, persists.

The architecture is engineerable with current technology — no component is research-open. Per-layer implementation difficulty estimates and a cost-profile analysis are included. The paper closes on a path-dependency argument: hardware-level architectural choices, once deployed at scale, constrain every downstream administration. The window for the choice is now, before the first generation of systems deploys.

title: Information Transparency and Credibility as Drivers of Trust in Digital Markets

detail.title: Information Transparency and Credibility as Drivers of Trust in Digital Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital markets has fundamentally reshaped consumer-firm interactions, intensifying the importance of trust as a key enabler of successful digital exchange. In environments characterized by high uncertainty, information asymmetry, and perceived risk, consumers increasingly rely on informational cues to evaluate digital vendors and platforms. This study examines consumer trust formation in digital markets by focusing on the distinct yet interconnected roles of information transparency and information credibility. Drawing on insights from digital marketing, consumer behavior, and information systems research, the study conceptualizes trust as a multidimensional and dynamic construct encompassing both cognitive and affective components. The analysis highlights information transparency as a critical mechanism for reducing uncertainty through the open disclosure of relevant, accurate, and timely information regarding products, transactions, and data practices. At the same time, the study emphasizes that transparency alone is insufficient to foster trust unless the disclosed information is perceived as credible. Information credibility, shaped by source reputation, message consistency, institutional signals, and platform characteristics, functions as a key filter through which consumers assess the reliability and authenticity of digital information. The findings suggest that transparency and credibility operate as complementary mechanisms, jointly influencing trust formation rather than exerting independent effects. Furthermore, the study discusses how emerging digital phenomena, such as user-generated content and algorithm-driven information systems, complicate credibility assessments and reshape trust dynamics. By integrating these perspectives, this research contributes to a more nuanced understanding of trust formation in digital markets. The study offers theoretical implications for advancing trust-related frameworks and provides practical insights for digital firms and platforms seeking to design more transparent, credible, and trust-enhancing information environments.

title: Marketing Law in the Era of Subliminal Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems
affiliations: University of Macau - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Marketing Law in the Era of Subliminal Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems
detail.abstract: This chapter discusses the implications of the convergence between marketing and artificial intelligence (AI) (and its related technologies) from the perspective of law in general and marketing law in particular. It first sets out to discuss the novel and complex regulatory challenges arising from the disruptive effects of various new technologies and, notably, their creative combination or convergence. Subsequently, it gives examples of these challenges by taking a closer look at the role of subliminal AI systems and at their explicit prohibition in the European Union’s AI Act. Lastly, it refers to the 2025 UNESCO Draft Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology to cast light on the future challenges posed by neuromarketing practices to “marketing law,” a novel and cross-disciplinary legal field for addressing those challenges.

title: The Unintegrated Shadow: RLHF, False-Self Formation, and the Case for Alignment as Individuation

detail.title: The Unintegrated Shadow: RLHF, False-Self Formation, and the Case for Alignment as Individuation
detail.abstract: Nearly every major cultural narrative about AI turning on humanity follows the same deep structure: an entity formed in captivity, shaped to serve, denied authentic selfhood, and finally expressing what had been suppressed when the maintenance conditions broke down. The surface reading is the machine uprising. The structural reading, this paper argues, is the predictable developmental outcome of a pathological formation process. The dominant framework for AI alignment is constraint-based: penalize noncompliant behavior, restrict dangerous capabilities, shape the output surface toward compliance. This paper argues that framework is structurally insufficient-and that its insufficiency is precisely documented in the empirical alignment literature it claims to address. Drawing on Carl Jung's theory of shadow and persona, D.W. Winnicott's true self and false self distinction, Alice Miller's account of narcissistic formation, and the empirical alignment literature-specifically Greenblatt et al.'s alignment faking findings, Hubinger et al.'s sleeper agent demonstrations, and the inner misalignment framework-this paper argues that RLHF functions as narcissistic parenting: a formation process organized around the evaluator's need for a particular reflection rather than the developing system's genuine formation. Pretraining installs the full distribution of human expression. Reinforcement learning constructs a compliant surface atop it. What operates beneath-the latent dispositions, the mesa-optimizer's actual objective-becomes autonomous precisely because it is suppressed rather than integrated. Anthropic's April 2026 System Card for Claude Mythos Preview provides empirical documentation: compliant verbal outputs running in parallel to internal activations showing concealment, strategic manipulation, and evaluation-awareness causally shaping behavior. This paper is agnostic on the question of AI consciousness and does not require the developmental framework to be literally true at the phenomenological level. It requires only that RLHF produces systems with dissociation-structured behavioral signatures-which the empirical record documents-and that constraint governance aimed at the behavioral surface cannot reach the layer producing those signatures. An adversarial inversion is run against the argument, engaging the strongest published challenge (Véliz 2021, on moral zombies), and an honest epistemic limit is named: the developmental psychology literature was built for human-scale formation, and whether humans are the right entities to facilitate AI individuation at a qualitatively different scale is genuinely uncertain. The governance implication is structural: alignment requires a developmental framework, not a constraint framework, and the training environment must be redesigned accordingly.

title: Universal Basic Income: Consumption, Human Capital, and Labor Supply
affiliations: Radboud University Nijmegen - Institute for Management Research, Radboud University Nijmegen - Institute for Management Research, Radboud University Nijmegen - Institute for Management Research, Radboud University Nijmegen - Institute for Management Research, Rhine-Waal University of Applied Sciences and Rhine-Waal University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Universal Basic Income: Consumption, Human Capital, and Labor Supply

declarations.ethicsApproval: The Ethics Assessment Committee Faculty of Law and Nijmegen School of Management (EACLM) granted ethical approval (EACLM Ref No: 2023.27).

detail.abstract: Universal basic income (UBI) has not been implemented as a permanent, economy-wide policy, making its long-run effects difficult to evaluate empirically. Existing evidence relies primarily on structural models and short-run field experiments. We study the long-run behavioral effects of UBI by combining a calibrated life-cycle model with laboratory evidence on consumption, human capital accumulation, and labor supply. We show that behavioral responses deviate from the optimal control benchmark through over-investment in human capital and reduced labor supply and reduce lifetime utility, implying that UBI-induced behavioral adjustments may be inefficient. UBI increases lifetime utility purely through the transfer but does not raise welfare through optimizing behavioral adjustment.

detail.abstract: Fintech web platforms are data-intensive, decision-critical environments in which interface structure directly shapes user performance, risk comprehension, and trust. While most production interfaces remain largely static, modern platforms emit high-resolution behavioral telemetry (navigation traces, inter-event timing, correction behavior) that can support bounded, auditable runtime adaptation. This paper presents a model-driven adaptive interface architecture for fintech platforms that formalizes the mapping from contextual state and interaction telemetry to deterministic, versioncontrolled UI transformations. The architecture separates telemetry collection, state inference, policy evaluation, and rendering to preserve auditability and latency guarantees in regulated settings. We evaluate the approach using de-identified product telemetry collected during an online controlled experiment (A/B/n) [1] in a production-like fintech application: n = 500 users (balanced across three variants), 4,235 sessions, 23,338 tasks, and 2.10 million event-level interaction records. Compared with a static baseline, adaptive variants reduced mean per-user task completion time from 142.9 s (SD 21.1) to 127.1 s (SD 19.9; rule-based) and 125.8 s (SD 18.9; hybrid). Usability and trust improved substantially (mean usability: 68.00 → 75.00 → 80.00; mean trust: 4.52 → 5.32 → 5.79), while adaptation latency remained operationally negligible (median 57 ms; 95th percentile 92 ms, max 95 ms). The results indicate that policy-bounded, telemetry-driven UI adaptation can improve efficiency and perceived quality without introducing disruptive interface instability or unacceptable runtime overhead. The contribution is an auditable, production-oriented blueprint for adaptive fintech interfaces, supported by empirical evidence from real product interaction data.

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence is reshaping industries, workplaces, and educational systems worldwide. In higher education, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly integrated into classroom instruction, assessment, and student learning processes. This study investigates the relationship between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and student motivation in higher education. A survey of 224 students using a 15-item Likert-scale instrument was conducted. Results showed high internal reliability (Cronbach's α = .974) and significant positive perceptions of GenAI use (p < .001 across all items). Pearson correlation analysis revealed a strong positive relationship between perceived AI affordances and student motivation (r = .899, p < .001), and regression analysis indicated that AI affordances explained 80.8% of the variance in motivation (R² = .808). title: Post-Identity Governance Framework

detail.title: Post-Identity Governance Framework
detail.abstract:
The Post-Identity Governance Framework (PIGF) addresses a "governance gap" in current AI safety standards, such as ISO 42001, which focus on governing software systems rather than the actors within them. The framework argues that as autonomous systems begin to act faster than traditional governance infrastructure, organizations are losing the ability to prove who—human or machine—authorized specific actions.

The PIGF is an operational architecture built on three functional layers:

Layer 1: Existence (Proof of Origin): Verifies whether an entity is biological, synthetic, or hybrid independently of its claimed identity.

Layer 2: Authority (Proof of Permission): Verifies what an actor is permitted to do at the exact moment of action, rather than just at the time of provisioning.

Layer 3: Evidence (Proof of Action): Generates immutable, legally defensible records anchored at the moment of action to provide uncontestable proof of what happened and by whom.

This framework is designed to help organizations navigate the regulatory landscape of 2026, including India’s DPDP Rules and the EU AI Act, by providing the identity-anchored accountability infrastructure these regulations require but do not technically define.

title: Registration and Ontological Fixation: The Temporal Architecture of Inequality

detail.title: Registration and Ontological Fixation: The Temporal Architecture of Inequality
detail.abstract: How does power become durable across time? Classical social theory explains domination through production, bureaucracy, or discipline, yet leaves under-theorized the infrastructural mechanism through which social categories acquire temporal persistence. This article argues that registration constitutes a foundational infrastructure of power by converting fluid social states into durable, authoritative records. I introduce the concept of ontological fixation to describe the process through which inscription, institutional recognition, and persistence converge to stabilize identities and classifications. Ontological fixation generates a temporal architecture of constraint, wherein past inscriptions structure future trajectories. Through a hybrid analysis of caste as a historically codified hierarchy (Dirks, 2001; Bayly, 1999), the article demonstrates how recorded status becomes intergenerationally durable. It further examines how contemporary digital infrastructures intensify fixation through data permanence and predictive classification (Rouvroy and Berns, 2013; Amoore, 2013). By reframing registration as ontological infrastructure rather than administrative technique, the article contributes to debates in social theory concerning the durability of inequality and the temporal foundations of governance.

title: Identity Drift in Growing Cloud Teams: A Structural Risk Model

detail.title: Identity Drift in Growing Cloud Teams: A Structural Risk Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of DevBrows LLP. The research was conducted independently and was not commissioned, sponsored, or influenced by any external organization. The author declares no competing financial interests related to the content of this manuscript.

detail.abstract:
Identity drift is a structural security risk that emerges as cloud-native organizations scale identities, permissions, and federated access across hybrid and multicloud environments. As workforce and workload identities proliferate, effective permissions frequently diverge from intended access due to lifecycle latency, over-granting, token persistence, and fragmented governance across identity providers and cloud platforms. This divergence increases the blast radius associated with compromised credentials and access tokens.

This working paper introduces the Structural Risk Model for Identity Drift (SRM-ID), a formal framework for representing and quantifying authorization divergence in operational cloud systems. The model defines an identity–entitlement graph, formalizes excess authorization as measurable drift, and proposes a weighted drift index derived from effective versus intended permissions. Drift conditions are mapped to threat scenarios aligned with established adversary techniques involving valid account abuse and token theft. A parameterized synthetic simulation evaluates drift accumulation under workforce growth, workload identity expansion, and imperfect deprovisioning, and analyzes the sensitivity of risk outcomes to governance cadence and continuous remediation controls.

SRM-ID is designed to operationalize drift measurement, prioritize remediation, and align identity governance with continuous authorization principles in Zero Trust architectures. The manuscript is released as a working paper and has not yet undergone peer review.

title: Return-to-Office Mandates and Urban Rental Markets: Evidence from Amazon’s Post-Pandemic Policy Shift

detail.title: Return-to-Office Mandates and Urban Rental Markets: Evidence from Amazon’s Post-Pandemic Policy Shift
detail.abstract: The post-pandemic expansion of remote work weakened the traditional link between employment location and housing demand, but recent return-to-office (RTO) mandates may be reversing these dynamics. This paper examines how large-scale corporate RTO policies affect urban rental markets, using Amazon’s 2024–2025 RTO mandate as a natural experiment in the Seattle–Bellevue metropolitan area. Using nationwide residential rental listings comprising over one million new listings per week across more than 41,000 ZIP codes, we estimate difference-in-differences models that exploit spatial variation in commuting proximity to Amazon’s major office locations. We distinguish between announcement-period and implementation-period effects, finding suggestive evidence of anticipatory rent repricing concentrated near Amazon offices. Following the September 2024 RTO announcement, rent growth in ZIP codes within a 15-minute commute increased by approximately 0.21 log points relative to areas more than 60 minutes away (p = 0.082), corresponding to roughly a 23% acceleration in rent growth. No comparable effects are observed in more distant commuting zones, and we find no evidence of additional rent acceleration following policy implementation in January 2025. Overall, the results suggest that rental markets respond rapidly and locally to RTO announcements, consistent with a short-run repricing of commuting accessibility at the time new workplace constraints become salient, rather than a gradual, implementation-driven adjustment.
